item.title: Canada, U.S. ‘very close’ to finalizing trade deal, LeBlanc says. Live updates here.
item.description: Canadian trade representatives have arrived in Washington for more talks amid a tentative trade deal with the U.S. It comes after U.S. President Donald Trump delayed imposing new tariffs on Canada ...
item.dc:creator: CTVNews.ca Staff
item.content:encoded: Canadian trade representatives have arrived in Washington for more talks amid a tentative trade deal with the U.S. It comes after U.S. President Donald Trump delayed imposing new tariffs on Canada until later this week. LeBlanc and Chief Negotiator Janice Charette were seen arriving shortly after noon ET at the U.S. Trade Representative offices to meet with their American counterpart Jamieson Greer. They were joined by Canada’s Ambassador to the U.S. Mark Wiseman and Prime Minister Mark Carney’s chief of staff Marc-André Blanchard. “I’m always looking forward to be back at work,” LeBlanc told reporters. “Janice is with me, some friends from Ottawa. This is great.” Canada and the U.S. now have until Saturday to reach a deal before Trump imposes 50 per cent tariffs on Canadian goods. In a Truth Social post Tuesday night, the U.S. president stated that he would delay his tariffs for three days and added that the two countries have reached a tentative deal. He also said that the Keystone XL pipeline “may be awoken from the grave.” Carney’s own statement released Wednesday did not mention a deal or a pipeline, but said that “substantial progress has been made.” Follow along for key updates: LeBlanc on trade deal: ‘We’re very close’ Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc shared an update following a more than three-hour meeting with U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer in Washington on Thursday, saying they are “very close” to an agreement. “We continue to make progress, and we’re going to stay here and do the work that’s necessary until we get to that point,” LeBlanc said to reporters, while also describing the meeting as “long” and “detailed.” Chief Trade Negotiator Janice Charette, Canadian Ambassador to the U.S. Mark Wiseman and Prime Minister Mark Carney’s Chief of Staff Marc-André Blanchard were also involved in the meeting. Stephanie Ha, bureau manager, Ottawa News Bureau All provinces agreed to restock U.S. liquor: N.L. premier Newfoundland and Labrador Premier Tony Wakeham says Canada’s premiers have agreed to return U.S. alcohol to store shelves as part of the tentative trade deal with the U.S. He said the prime minister is confident an agreement will be reached and that “as part of this agreement, he asked all of the provinces, as a sign of good faith, ‘would we put U.S. liquor back on our shelves,’ and we all agreed.” Several of the premiers have not commented publicly on the issue. U.S. alcohol products remain off the shelves in every province except Alberta and Saskatchewan. Tiffany Hendsbee, CTV News supervising multiplatform writer Wab Kinew on U.S. booze: ‘Don’t buy it’ Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew said the tentative trade deal that could see U.S. alcohol returned to store shelves “will not be right for him,” while urging Canadians to keep buying domestic products. “If we put the booze back on the shelves, don’t buy it. Let it sit on the shelf where the liquor mart employees will be putting it, and buy the Canadian stuff instead,” he told reporters in Winnipeg. While Newfoundland and Labrador Premier Tony Wakeham said all provinces agreed to return U.S. alcohol to store shelves, Kinew seemingly took a stand against the decision, telling Canadians, “let’s send a message that even though the prime minister and the government of Canada might think it’s important for us to put things back on the shelf… that we don’t like Donald Trump’s approach to trade or his way of treating Canada.” Kinew said that if the deal goes ahead, U.S. alcohol could return to Manitoba shelves “relatively quickly,” with some returning “within a few days,” while full catalogues could take “a few weeks” due to labelling standards. Kinew reiterated his opposition to the agreement, saying: “No, the deal will not be right for me. I would expect, but it’s not about me. It’s about Team Canada.” Kayla Thompson, CTVNews.ca journalist Read CTV News Winnipeg’s full story here ‘Canadians won’t like it, but they will accept it’: Scott Reid CTV News political commentator Scott Reid says Manitoba’s premier may have a good sense of the public’s mood on this tentative deal between Canada and the United States. When Kinew suggested Canadians avoid American alcohol after it returns to store shelves, Reid says he was “very clearly expressing his disfavour about doing anything that smacks of concession toward Donald Trump,” adding that it “may be a taste of what the prime minister can expect from a lot of Canadians.” Reid, who served as director of communications for former prime minister Paul Martin, suggests the Carney government will sell the agreement by saying it’s the best deal possible. “Canadians won’t like it, but they will accept it,” Reid said. “I think they’re still at a stage where this issue is so complex, the stakes are so high, and the issues are so complicated, that they are willing to defer to Mark Carney.” Scott Ferguson, news director for CTV News Centralized Writing Service Sectoral tariffs reduced: sources Multiple sources tell CTV News there are reductions in sectoral tariffs, such as steel and aluminum, as part of the agreement with the United States, but none of the sources knew the scope of those reductions. As for how the public will respond, sources also tell CTV News the details of those sectorial tariffs will “make or break the deal” politically for Prime Minister Mark Carney. CTV News Ottawa Bureau Canada may end up with lowest tariff impact: N.L. premier The deal won’t eliminate U.S. tariffs, but it could ensure that Canada has the lowest impact compared to other affected countries, according to the Newfoundland and Labrador premier. Wakeham divulged as much in an interview with CTV News Channel on Thursday, sharing what the prime minister told premiers in a virtual meeting the previous day. He said he stood by Carney’s approach to negotiations. “I believe in the Team Canada approach ... and I look forward to a successful negotiation by the prime minister and his team,” Wakeham said. Devika Desai, CTVNews.ca journalist PM Carney speaks with Mexican president Carney spoke with Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum on Thursday about Mexico’s support in combating wildfires and progress on cross-border trade. According to a statement from Prime Minister’s Office, Carney thanked Sheinbaum for deploying more than 400 firefighters and support personnel. The two leaders also discussed ongoing developments affecting North American trade. “(Carney and Sheinbaum) underscored the importance of renewing the Canada-United States-Mexico Agreement (CUSMA) as soon as possible to provide greater certainty for North American businesses and workers,” the statement read. Both leaders agreed to stay in close contact. Kayla Thompson, CTVNews.ca journalist Don’t underestimate Trump: Former Trudeau adviser The U.S. president may appear to be in hot water leading up to the midterm elections, but a former Trudeau adviser cautioned against underestimating him. “He has managed to be a bit of a comeback kid on several occasions politically, even when the tide seems to be against him,” Diamond Isinger, former Canada-U.S. relations special adviser under the Trudeau administration, told CTV News Channel on Thursday. However, rising affordability costs in the U.S. could work in Canada’s favour, as they can be at least partly attributed to the tariffs on other countries, she added. She added that it’s unsurprising that some premiers, like the Manitoba leader, may still advocate to their residents to shop local even if the ban on alcohol is lifted. “One of the things that Kinew illustrated ... is the reality that even if provinces do restock that liquor tomorrow or next week, the consumer behaviours and the interest in purchasing American has potentially rapidly declined on part of Canadians,” Isinger said. “So whether or not the U.S. will look favorably at the fact that we are restocking their products, but not actively purchasing them, remains to be seen.” Devika Desai, CTVNews.ca journalist ‘Can’t make a good deal with a bad person’: Manitoba’s Kinew Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew told Winnipeg’s 680 CJOB Thursday it looks like there will be a lower tariff on the Gerdau steel mill in Selkirk, Man., but it is still “way higher than it was two years ago.” Kinew added that Carney asked the provinces to return American booze to the shelves, and told them they could blame him if they receive any backlash for the decision. “If we do end up putting the booze back on the shelves, like I’ve said. we still have to see some of the details here, we reserve the right to take it back off again, because we know that this guy is very erratic, the American president, and he may go back on his word, as he’s done countless times,” Kinew said in his radio interview. The Manitoba premier also quoted famed investor Warren Buffett in saying “you can’t make a good deal with a bad person,” once again referring to Trump as “Jeffery Epstein’s best friend” and blaming the president for high gas prices brought on by the war in Iran. The Canadian Press Read the full article here Carney speaks with Quebec premier Prime Minister Mark Carney spoke with Quebec Premier Christine Frechette again today, a source with knowledge tells CTV News. It comes a day after Carney met with his cabinet and the country’s premiers following the news about a potential trade deal. Kayla Thompson, CTVNews.ca journalist ‘Sounds like Canada has given up’: Scheer Conservative House leader Andrew Scheer says although he’s “cautiously optimistic,” he is “worried” about what Carney may be giving to avoid 50 per cent tariffs. “My hope is that we get an elimination of tariffs. It sounds like Canada has given up,” Scheer told CTV Your Morning Saskatchewan Thursday morning. Scheer said the big question is whether Carney comes back with zero tariffs, or the baseline of 25 per cent. “If he comes back with a deal where there’s still 25 per cent tariffs on steel and aluminum, there’s going to be a lot of workers here in Regina (and) across the country that will be scratching their heads, saying, ‘You know, Mark Carney seems to have given up quite a lot.’” Scheer also echoed criticism raised by Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre, saying Carney has failed to brief the Opposition on negotiations. “We’re in a little bit of a wait-and-see mode. We’ll see what the final deal is.” Kayla Thompson, CTVNews.ca journalist Agriculture the ‘No. 1 issue’: U.S. secretary Brooke Rollins, the U.S. secretary of agriculture, says President Trump remains “very focused on Canada, specifically as it relates to dairy,” as well as other issues. Speaking to reporters on Thursday, Rollins said she and Trump believe the new deal will make farmers happy. “My great friend Scott Bessent … Howard Lutnick, (and) Jamieson Greer, they have made, alongside President Trump and with his direction, agriculture as the No. 1 issue as they are moving into these rooms and have these discussions” she said. “The president has not been shy about his frustration with Canada and especially with dairy and what Canada’s rules have done to our incredible dairy producers in America.” Kayla Thompson, CTVNews.ca journalist Why is the U.S. mad about who sells cheese in Canada? Cheese has once again become a hot topic in the Canada-U.S. trade dispute. While officials work to lower sectoral tariffs on Canadian steel and aluminum, the U.S. wants Canada to change its strict rules on importing cheese, which a Canadian agricultural economist warns heavily against. “It’s not in the Canadian interest,” explains Al Mussell, a prominent Canadian agricultural economist and policy analyst. Mussell explains that the U.S. wants more control over who can access Canadian retailers directly, so they can export some of their premium products to Canada. Last month, U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order threatening a 50 per cent tariff on Canadian goods, including the country’s dairy sector. Anam Khan, BNN Bloomberg journalist Read the full article here ‘In the end game’: diplomat Negotiations are nearing a close, Canada’s U.K. high commissioner says, judging from the joint statements given by Canadian and U.S. trade reps on the state of talks this week. Ralph Goodale, who is a member of the prime minister’s advisory council on Canada-U.S. economic relations, pointed to a media appearance by Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc and his U.S. counterpart Jamieson Greer on Wednesday in Washington. “The two of them together commenting on what they were presenting as a successful negotiation .... we’re very much in the end game,” Goodale told CTV News Channel on Thursday. Getting the premiers to agree on the deal may sound “impossible,” he added, if not for the display of “national cohesion” by Canadians. “That’s an incentive for all politicians ... to pull together,” he said. Yet, the “antipathy” developed towards the U.S. could still make it a “hard sell,” Goodale noted. “Canadians will be wary,” he acknowledged. “...The reliability of the arrangement is always going to be a question in Canadians’ minds.” Devika Desai, CTVNews.ca journalist Keep the quota system: Dairy farmer A Quebec dairy farmer wants to keep the quota system used in Canada’s supply management “intact” in trade negotiations with the U.S. “We have a lot of money invested in that,” Angus MacKinnon told CTV News Channel on Thursday. Canadian dairy farmers produce supply according to quotas assigned by the federal government and are paid regulated pricing that factors in production costs, farm labour and capital expenditures. “The stability that quota brings to the dairy industry is reflected in the community,” MacKinnon said. The tariffs haven’t impacted income, he added. Last year Canada conceded four per cent of national production to the U.S. in trade talks but said it would not negotiate more on market access, he added. “I’m investing a tremendous amount of money in the construction of a barn,” he said. “So I need a positive outlook for the future.” Devika Desai, CTVNews.ca journalist Softwood lumber is ‘outlier’ in trade talks: expert It’s still unclear how softwood lumber will be treated in ongoing trade negotiations, according to an industry expert. But Derek Nighbor, president and CEO of Forest Products Association of Canada says that he’s “optimistic.” The industry employs almost 200,000 people in Canada, “more than auto, steel and aluminum combined,” he told CTV News Channel on Thursday. “We’re still hopeful in the home stretch here,” he added. Ideally, Sections 338 and 232 which directly impact the industry would be eliminated, he said. “If we can see those tariffs go away and if we can get a commitment to see Canada and the United States get back to the table to negotiate an agreement on softwood, I think that would be a pretty good outcome,” he said. Under existing tariffs, the industry is losing market share to the Americans, Austrians, Swedes and Germans, as the Europeans only bear a 15 per cent premium, he said. “We’ve heard the president talk this week a lot about fairness and treating Canada more equally in different segments like other countries,” he said. “Lumber is clearly an outlier, and we’d like to see that gap close very much.” Devika Desai, CTVNews.ca journalist Foreign affairs minister travels to Washington Anita Anand, Canada’s minister of foreign affairs, will travel to Washington on Thursday to meet her U.S. counterpart, Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Global Affairs Canada stated in a press release on Thursday that the two will discuss “continental security and other global priorities” but did not share more details. According to a Thursday schedule released by the U.S. Department of State, Anand will meet with Rubio at 1:30 p.m. EDT at the White House. The meeting will be closed to the media. Anand’s office has confirmed the meeting is not related to trade negotiations. Devika Desai, CTVNews.ca journalist Premiers are optimistic Some premiers say they’re optimistic about Canada’s progress in reaching a trade deal to avoid punishing tariffs from the United States, while others say they’re waiting for more details about the agreement. Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston told reporters Wednesday that he was “optimistic” about the deal, adding that Prime Minister Mark Carney has asked provinces to restock American alcohol on their shelves. B.C.’s David Eby said that while no agreement will offer everything the country is hoping for, the federal government has made substantial progress across strategic sectors. Scott Moe of Saskatchewan said Wednesday that he hopes both countries can negotiate a deal that would reduce U.S. tariffs on Canadian steel, aluminum, autos and lumber. Quebec Premier Christine Fréchette told reporters it was too soon to make a judgment call about the deal, adding that she needed more information to see whether it’s positive for her province. The Canadian Press Province needs to diversify: N.S. premier Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston said that Canada’s trade dispute with the U.S. has been a wake-up call to diversify the province’s economy. Houston was responding late Wednesday to a potential Canada-U.S. trade deal from Banff, Alta., where he’s promoting energy projects at an industry conference. He said the dispute has taught the province it needs to develop more diverse trading partners for sectors like seafood and agriculture, though the U.S. market is still important. He said Nova Scotia also has to be more self-sufficient, especially on the energy file. “The whole experience has taught us something really important about diversification and pushing Nova Scotian opportunities,” Houston told reporters. " “That’s why I’m in Alberta right now talking about Nova Scotia gas and ... oil and ... opportunities. Diversifying our trading partners for our markets and seafood and agriculture and all kinds of things.” The Canadian Press, Read the full article here Reducing steel, aluminum tariffs ‘extremely important’: expert An international trade lawyer says an agreement that includes reductions to Section 232 tariffs on steel and aluminum will be “extremely important” for sectors that have been “really suffering.” “If we can regain access to the United States market, our producers are going to be in a much better place, and might even have a competitive advantage compared with the rest of the world,” William Pellerin told CTV News Channel on Thursday. While neither side has confirmed details involving dairy, comments made by Trump on Wednesday that the new agreement is “great for our farmers” leads Pellerin to suspect “minor concessions” have been made. Left off the negotiating table so far is softwood lumber, which Pellerin said is a disadvantage for Quebec, British Columbia and Alberta lumber producers. “It would have been nice relief, but I think we probably didn’t have enough cards to play to also get some relief on that sector,” he said. Kayla Thompson, CTVNews.ca journalist Keystone XL benefits both: expert “It’s really one of those unique cases where I think both countries benefit,” said Dennis McConaghy, a former Canadian energy executive, on Thursday. In an interview with CTV Your Morning, McConaghy explained that Canada would benefit economically if Keystone XL were revived, since Canadian heavy oil suits U.S. refineries. “Now the argument has always been Canada might gain more economic margin by sending its incremental oil production to the West Coast,” McConaghy said. “Of course, that means you have to be able to get a pipeline built to the West Coast, and that’s always had obvious risks.” Devika Desai, CTVNews.ca journalist Avoid ‘escalation’: agri-food expert Canada’s agri-food exporters are “optimistic” about Trump’s tariff pause as it abated a potential “escalatory spiral” that could have hurt business, a Canadian expert says. Michael Harvey, the executive director of the Canadian Agri-Food Trade Alliance, told CTV News Channel on Wednesday that while the industry isn’t directly impacted by the tariffs, there has been “an increasing level of political risk that’s made it difficult to make business decisions to invest.” “Our concern has been an escalatory spiral where there could be across-the-board tariffs that would hit,” he said. Despite becoming a more difficult market to work with, the U.S. still makes up 70 per cent of Canada’s agri-food exports, he added. “We have to manage these contradictory ... situations.” “Our situation is of confidence, but not too much confidence.” Devika Desai, CTVNews.ca journalist PM Carney asks for return of U.S. booze Following a virtual first ministers meeting, Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston said Prime Minister Mark Carney asked the provincial leaders “to return the U.S. alcohol to the shelf.” In a virtual media conference on Wednesday, Houston said the ask is “something that came directly out of the negotiating table,” and is “something that (he) would be willing to do for the prime minister at this point in time.” “Whether Nova Scotians or whether Canadians will actually buy it when it gets back on the shelves, that’s a whole other discussion,” he added. Kayla Thompson, CTVNews.ca journalist Provincial sources: trade deal not done Multiple provincial sources are sharing cautious optimism with CTV News following a briefing with Carney on the tentative trade deal between Canada and the U.S. However, they also emphasized that the deal is not done yet. In a post to Truth Social late Tuesday, Trump said the countries “have a deal,” but sources say that characterization is not accurate and further negotiations are ongoing. The provincial sources also tell CTV News that Carney personally asked the premiers to return U.S. alcohol to store shelves. He even told them he will bear any public pushback if that happens. According to a recent Nanos Research survey, most Canadians say they won’t purchase U.S. booze if it returns to stores. Stephanie Ha, bureau manager, Ottawa News Bureau With files from CTV News’ chief political correspondent Vassy Kapelos

item.title: Why U.S. Treasury Secretary Bessent’s moves to calm the bond market haven’t worked so far
item.description: The yield on the 10-year Treasury note, a key benchmark for mortgage rates, rose back to 4.69 per cent Thursday.
item.dc:creator: The Associated Press
item.content:encoded: WASHINGTON — Interest rates rebounded Thursday despite efforts by U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to put a lid on longer-term borrowing costs, a sign Wall Street investors remain worried about burgeoning government debt, heavy borrowing by tech firms, and the Federal Reserve’s commitment to fighting inflation. The yield on the 10-year Treasury note, a key benchmark for mortgage rates, rose back to 4.69 per cent Thursday. That is nearly where it stood early Wednesday before Bessent surprised financial markets by announcing that Treasury would double the size of a bond buyback program starting next month to US$4 billion per operation from US$2 billion. The buybacks are intended to reduce the supply of 10-year to 30-year bonds and boost their prices. Yields on bonds fall when their prices rise. Bessent said Thursday on CNBC that the bond repurchase program could be larger than US$4 billion. “We have a big toolkit so we’ll see,” Bessent said. “We believe that the yields don’t reflect the underlying fundamentals.” Rising bond yields push up borrowing costs for consumers and businesses, and the Trump administration has set reducing interest rates as a top goal. Home purchases have slumped as mortgage rates have moved higher this year. U.S. President Donald Trump has often demanded that the Federal Reserve lower rates, but the ongoing increases are driven primarily by financial markets. The 30-year bond yield rose to 5.23 per cent Thursday, down only slightly from a 19-year high reached Tuesday. U.S. Treasury’s move doesn’t fix the fundamental problems spooking the bond market Bessent also said the Trump administration would announce a new effort to reduce the government’s budget deficit, possibly by Monday. He argued that the deficit will peak this year, in part because it has been driven higher by tariff refunds, a temporary factor. While the deficit has been huge for years, overall debt topped US$40 trillion on Wednesday, a staggering record that arrived just months after the national debt first blew past the US$39 trillion mark in April. And the Congressional Budget Office estimated earlier this week that the annual gap between government revenue and spending would top US$2 trillion this year, a remarkable number outside of recessions. But Gennadiy Goldberg, head of U.S. rates strategy at TD Securities, said reducing the deficit is mostly up to Congress, rather than the Treasury Department. “What we are seeing is the market is still a little bit skeptical that Treasury can and will be able to backstop some of these moves,” Goldberg said. Another factor pushing yields higher is how much debt Big Tech companies are raising to build AI data centers. Their deluge of bond offerings is giving bond investors more to choose from, which lowers prices for bonds and pushes up their yields. Investors are skeptical of the Fed’s willingness to fight inflation Inflation also remains a threat because oil prices keep climbing on uncertainty about when the war with Iran will let tankers freely exit the Persian Gulf again. They rose again Thursday after Trump threatened Iran with “the MOST CRUSHING ECONOMIC OPERATION EVER TAKEN AGAINST ANY COUNTRY.” The price of Brent crude oil is near US$94 per barrel, compared with roughly US$72 before the start of the war. The Fed typically combats inflation by raising its benchmark interest rate to slow borrowing and spending and cool the economy. Yet new Fed chair Kevin Warsh hasn’t signaled whether the Fed will take such a step. At his most recent press conference in late July, he sowed confusion about whether he sees higher rates as the right approach. He also suggested the Fed could soon switch the gauge it uses to monitor inflation, which it seeks to keep at 2 per cent. Inflation has topped that level for more than five years, and was 3.7 per cent in June, according to the Fed’s preferred measure. Mark Cabana, head of U.S. rates strategy at Bank of America Securities, said that a key reason for higher borrowing costs “is just elevated uncertainty about how the Fed is going to contain inflation” and what it will do “in case things don’t go to plan.” Yet Warsh has underscored he doesn’t want to provide such signals because he wants financial markets to set interest rates based on economic conditions, not on what it expects the Fed to do. Bessent’s intervention appears to be at cross-purposes with that goal, since markets are now considering what next steps Treasury might take to contain rates. The rise in rates has put pressure on Warsh to clarify his approach when he delivers a high-profile speech next Friday at an annual Fed conference in Jackson Hole, Wyoming. “Now the ball is in the Fed’s court and the ball is really in Kevin Warsh’s hands,” Cabana said. “And the market is questioning, will Warsh respond? Will he articulate a better plan?” Warsh was appointed by Trump after his predecessor, Jerome Powell, finished his term in May. Trump relentlessly attacked Powell for not cutting rates, raising concerns that Warsh is inclined to reduce rates to placate Trump. Shorter-term bond yields dipped after the Fed’s July 28-29 rates meeting, while longer-term yields rose. It was an unusual reaction to a Fed meeting, according to strategists at BNP Paribas, and could suggest investors believe the Fed wants to keep its benchmark rate lower rather than higher. U.S. Treasury buyback is small compared to the size of the market While Bessent is talking about billions of dollars in bond buybacks, the Treasury market is so large that even purchases at that scale may not have much impact. Analysts at Macquarie, an investment bank, estimate that the U.S. government will need to issue nearly US$550 billion in bonds this quarter to finance its operations. History also shows that government interventions in the bond market have limited effects. “While such measures can reduce volatility and provide temporary relief, they have not permanently lowered borrowing costs when fiscal, inflation, or supply dynamics remained unfavorable,” according to strategists at UBS Wealth Management, pointing to prior examples from Japan and the United Kingdom. --- Christopher Rugaber And Stan Choe, The Associated Press

item.title: Why is the U.S. mad about who sells cheese in Canada?
item.description: Cheese has once again become a hot topic in the Canada-U.S. trade dispute. While officials work to lower sectoral tariffs on Canadian steel and aluminum, the U.S. wants Canada to change its strict ...
item.dc:creator: Anam Khan
item.content:encoded: Cheese has once again become a hot topic in the Canada-U.S. trade dispute. While officials work to lower sectoral tariffs on Canadian steel and aluminum, the U.S. wants Canada to change its strict rules on importing cheese, which a Canadian agricultural economist warns heavily against. “It’s not in the Canadian interest,” explains Al Mussell, a prominent Canadian agricultural economist and policy analyst. Last month, U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order threatening a 50 per cent tariff on Canada’s dairy sector, which is now in a three day suspension period as negotiations continue. Mussell explains that the U.S. wants more control over who can access Canadian retailers directly, so they can export some of their premium products to Canada. “Of course, that’s not how our system works,” he says, adding that allowing it would threaten Canadian processors and complicate the domestic raw milk allocation system. Canada currently gives dairy import quota access mainly to processors, while retailers are excluded under CUSMA. The U.S. argues that this restriction creates an unfair playing field because retailers are granted access under Canada’s trade agreement with the European Union. The U.S. administration says “Canada is discriminating against the commerce of the United States through Canada’s tariff-rate quota allocation measures imposed on U.S. cheeses of all types.” Canada and the U.S. have fought over this before The dispute over who gets access to Canada’s dairy quotas is not new. The U.S. first launched a formal dispute under CUSMA, arguing that Canada’s dairy import system shut out U.S. producers because it gave almost all its import permits to domestic dairy factories. After a trade panel ruled that this was unfair, Canada changed the rules to let other dairy businesses, like distributors, get the permits too. However, retailers remain excluded. When the U.S. challenged Canada again, arguing retailers should also be allowed direct access, the panel sided with Canada, saying it was in compliance with CUSMA. Mussell says the U.S. continuing to press the issue despite that ruling is not a good sign. “I think it goes far beyond cheese or dairy products,” he says. “When the President can come in and make threats that contravene a decision that the dispute panel under the CUSMA agreement rendered… that’s really troubling.” What happens if retailers get more access? Mussell says giving grocery retailers direct access would not increase the total amount of U.S. cheese entering Canada, since the quota is already essentially filled, but it could shift sales away from Canadian manufacturers. He says it could also complicate Canada’s supply management system because raw milk is allocated to processing plants on a regulated basis. “That could be costly to the Canadian dairy industry,” he says. Mussell also warns that giving grocery retailers more direct access to imports could strengthen their negotiating position with Canadian dairy suppliers. “Your’re kind of arming them in terms of the sorts of relations that they can have with their dairy suppliers,” he says. ‘Our national food sovereignty is not up for negotiation’ In response to the tariff threat, a joint letter by the Dairy Farmers of Canada and the Dairy Processors Association of Canada last week expressed disappointment that the dairy sector was dragged into a trade dispute once again. “Our national food sovereignty is not up for negotiation,” said David Wiens, president of DFC. “It is also clear that Canadians believe in the importance of having control over our food supply and ensuring that Canada’s strong domestic dairy sector is not compromised.” The trade relationship in dairy already “massively favours the U.S.” said Mathieu Frigon, president of the DPAC. “U.S. dairy exports to Canada far exceed Canadian dairy exports to the U.S. by more than $600 million annually and have increased by more than 150% since CUSMA came into effect,” said Frigon. What about the quality of U.S. dairy? Mussell says even if more U.S. milk entered Canada, there is a major difference between Canadian and U.S. dairy quality standards. “You could have milk that shipped under the U.S. Grade A that would not be saleable in any province in Canada,” he says. Moreover, he says a significant amount of American milk doesn’t even meet its own Grade A standard. “Is that product being exported to Canada, made from that milk? We don’t know. They don’t label. We have no way of knowing that,” says Mussell. He says federal funding for labs that monitor the U.S. milk testing system stopped last year. “What’s the nature of the safety and quality of product that we’re getting from the United States? I don’t know that we have an answer for that, and it’s concerning,” says Mussell.

item.title: WSP Global continues pursuit of deal to acquire Dutch engineering firm Arcadis
item.description: WSP Global Inc. is continuing its pursuit of Dutch engineering firm Arcadis NV even after its latest offer worth about $7.5 billion was rejected last month.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: MONTREAL — WSP Global Inc. is continuing its pursuit of Dutch engineering firm Arcadis NV even after its latest offer worth about $7.5 billion was rejected last month for being too low. In an update required by Dutch regulations, the Montreal-based firm confirmed Thursday its intention to continue to seek a combination with Arcadis through a friendly, recommended public offer. WSP says it remains convinced that a combination with Arcadis represents a “highly compelling opportunity.” The Canadian engineering form also says it continues to seek talks with Arcadis to determine whether a mutually agreeable transaction can be achieved. Last month, WSP made an offer of 51.50 euros per share for Arcadis, up from an earlier bid of 48.50 euros per share that Arcadis rejected. However, Arcadis said the improved offer continued to undervalue the company and was not in the best interest of its shareholders, employees, clients and other stakeholders. --- This report by The Canadian Press was first published Aug. 20, 2026.
